doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Staying away from 1960s modern jazz and anger in the music
summary: He walked away from Coltrane and Miles Davis-era anger, describes being welcomed in Harlem as a white player in 1958, and says jazz is music for everybody.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: When players in the 60s came along — Coltrane, Miles Davis — the music seemed to get, some of it, pretty angry. Was it something you listened to? Did it have an effect on you?

I just walked away from — I was not that interested. Some of the beautiful Miles Davis, you know the beautiful things, I loved it. The other agendas that go with the playing, the attitudes and things, I try not to let that get in the way of my playing. I think by that time I already had decided kind of where I was going to go musically and didn’t want to get into a lot of that, I thought it would mess my style. Of course I was working in the 60s, I was still working days, I hadn’t made my commitment to go full time. And it was very shaky to get into music. It was precarious. It was kind of dangerous to consider being a full time musician. And hearing how great these guys were, they weren’t all that successful financially so I didn’t go that route. When the time came, remember it was Benny Goodman called me to play with him. Red Balaban, who played in the Condon tradition was going to open a night club, he hired me to book his band, so I was very secure in the swing idiom and it’s almost like I didn’t want to go down that road. And the angriness that has taken hold in much of music and much of jazz and much of the music of today, I don’t want any part of it. When I came to New York in 1958 after college, I mean yes if I were a black at that time I probably would not be telling you the same thing I’d be telling you now. But for me, a white, I was welcomed. I mean I would see Al Casey up on St. Nicholas Avenue, I’d hire him on a job and take him and wait while he brought his guitar up and came back for his amp. I dated my wife in Harlem. We went to the Baby Grand. I was welcomed into the jazz community and there weren’t a lot of agendas going on at the time. Jazz was not black. Jazz was for everybody. Now it’s very polarized with what’s going on. So I don’t buy into all that anger. And jazz is European. I mean jazz, granted it started in the States, but you go to Europe and you’ve got some pretty fine players over there. Jazz is music. Music is for everybody. And it’s not our music. So the angriness never, I just walked away from it. I’m going through life once, I’m going to have fun. What other jobs can you think of where you go to work and everybody wants to have a good time. I mean how many people go to an office where it’s nothing but aggravation night and day. I go to a job and people really want to have a

great time. So let’s have a great time together. I don’t believe in goofing off or hacking around, I mean I’ve very, I set pretty high professional standards for myself and the fellows around me, but I mean let’s have a good time and play some darn good music.
